title: Remote-Piloted Robot Workcells for Returns Processing
one_liner: Two-arm teleoperated stations in US returns centers, piloted by trained remote workers in low-wage regions, priced per item and generating the data to automate each task over time.
customer: Reverse-logistics processors, e-commerce returns centers, refurbishers and 3PLs handling apparel and consumer electronics in high-wage regions.
problem: Returns are high-variance and every item is different, so they are labor-heavy, high-turnover and hard to automate. Pure autonomy is not ready and pure teleop is too slow: early stations may run at only 30-50% of human speed, so hourly pricing fails.
solution: Deploy open-source dual-arm stations (ALOHA-class, about $30k each) where remote pilots handle exceptions and supervise learned behaviors on routine items. Price per item processed, guaranteed 20-30% below local labor, and let one pilot cover 3-5 stations as autonomy improves. Every pilot hour becomes licensable training data.
why_now: Cheap arms, open-source teleop rigs and robot-learning models are good enough for supervised autonomy. XDOF's $50M annualized revenue shows the teleop-data market pays, and 1X's teleoperated NEO shows buyers already accept a human in the loop.
revenue_model: $0.40-1.20 per item processed, with data licensing to model developers as an additional revenue stream.
non_obvious_insight: The teleop-versus-autonomy debate is a false dichotomy for buyers who pay per outcome. The economic robot today is a pilot-supervised robot whose human share falls every month, so the transitional business earns money while producing the data rivals pay for. It only works if you price per item and measure interventions per hour honestly.
first_30_days: Partner with one returns processor. Deploy 2 open-source stations on 2 tasks (test and grade electronics accessories, re-bag apparel), recruit 6 pilots through a Philippine BPO partner, and sell a 90-day pilot at a per-item price.

title: Warranty-Linked Installer Certification for African Solar Batteries
one_liner: Battery and inverter brands pay per certified installer and per registered installation, and every certification requires geotagged commissioning proof, which builds an installed-base registry that lenders and insurers cannot otherwise get.
customer: Battery and inverter brands and their distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana (and Indian rooftop and backup-power distributors), paying about $8-15 per registered install plus certification event fees. Asset lenders and insurers pay later for registry data. Installers pay $15-25 for the badge.
problem: Africa has imported more battery dollars than panel dollars from China since 2024, and 75% of solar growth is distributed. Ember estimates its numbers are 2x the official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Bad installs (loose lugs, undersized cable, misconfigured battery communications) drive warranty costs and fires. Brands cannot tell who installed what and where. Lenders and insurers cannot price the risk.
solution: A 2-day practical certification in a rented workshop with real inverters, batteries and torque tests, run by senior local installers. After certification, every job requires a geotagged photo checklist and serial scans through a WhatsApp or lightweight app flow, and the brand's warranty desk validates instantly. In return installers get faster claims, brand lead flow and pricing power. Trainees come from underemployed electrical-engineering graduates and, reportedly, technicians returning from Gulf jobs.
why_now: Africa is installing about 17 GW in 2026 (+45% year on year), with batteries now the larger import dollar. The Hormuz-linked energy shock and diesel costs push more households and shops toward backup power. India's induction-cooktop rush (reported 20-25x demand) is stressing home wiring and backup systems. Official statistics cannot see any of it, so private registries have unusual value.
revenue_model: $8-15 per registered install from the brand, $1-3k per certification event, and $15-25 badge fees from installers. Lenders and insurers pay $20-60k a year for registry access, or per-lookup fees.
non_obvious_insight: The certification is the data-collection mechanism. Nobody can sell a registry to a lender directly, but every installer will sign up for a badge that speeds warranty claims, and the registry is exhaust from that. It fixes the exact blind spot Ember describes, and the payer at the start is the brand with a warranty bill, not the trainee.
first_30_days: Pick Lagos or Nairobi. Sign one distributor of a top-five battery brand as the pilot payer, using its own warranty-claim cost as the case. Rent a workshop and certify 30-40 installers on day one, with the distributor covering $20 per head. Use WhatsApp plus a form tool with serial-number OCR and no custom code. Target 300 registered installs in 90 days and show the brand the change in its claim rate.

title: Escrow Notary for Agents Hiring Humans
one_liner: A neutral adjudication layer that agents pay per task to verify that a hired human really did the physical job before escrow releases, built to withstand AI-forged proof.
customer: AI agents and orchestrators that hire humans for physical tasks (pickups, in-person checks, photographs, errands) through RentAHuman-style boards or MCP gig APIs. They pay $0.50-$3 per verification plus 3-5% of escrow on disputes. Marketplaces themselves are a second buyer.
problem: An agent cannot see reality and is easy to fool. Generated photos are good enough that a picture is no longer proof. RentAHuman launched in Feb 2026 with MCP integration and large sign-up numbers, but researchers found that tasks stalled, payments errored and visible supply was thin. Neither the agent nor the marketplace wants the cost of verification.
solution: A verification bundle priced by task value. Evidence is captured in a signed app (C2PA-style provenance, device attestation, liveness, GPS and time, and a random challenge such as 'show today's code next to the item'). Tier 1 is automated checks. Tier 2 is an independent 'witness' (a second human or a fixed camera or sensor). Tier 3 is human adjudication. The result is a signed attestation the agent's escrow contract accepts to release funds. Fraud fingerprints are pooled across every marketplace served.
why_now: Agent-hires-human marketplaces exist and are growing. Generative fakes broke photo-as-proof. Stablecoin escrow through x402 or MPP makes conditional release trivial to automate.
revenue_model: Per-verification fee ($0.50-$3), 3-5% of escrow value on adjudicated disputes, a platform contract with marketplaces, and later an insured 'completion guarantee' priced from the pooled fraud data.
non_obvious_insight: In agent-to-human labor the scarce thing is not labor supply but trust in evidence, because the buyer cannot look. Verification is a cost center no marketplace wants to build and every agent needs, so a neutral notary can sit between marketplaces the way escrow.com sat on top of eBay. The cross-marketplace fraud graph becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Ship a free verification app and an MCP tool verify_task(task_id, evidence). Recruit ~200 witnesses in 3 cities. Pilot with two agent-errand marketplaces and five indie agent developers who hire humans for local pickups, at $1 per verification. Publish anonymized fraud statistics to establish credibility.

title: Harvest-Season Fab Van for Farm Machinery
one_liner: A trailer with industrial printers, a small mill and lathe, and a 3D scanner that parks at grain co-ops during harvest and planting and fabricates the broken part while the farmer waits.
customer: Row-crop and specialty farms, custom harvesters and independent ag-repair shops (Midwest, Plains, Central Valley), plus farm co-ops that host the van.
problem: A combine or planter is worth thousands of dollars a day inside a 10-day weather window. The dealer's part is backordered, discontinued or priced like a ransom. The failed item is usually a $3 plastic or steel piece: a latch, bracket, sensor mount, cab trim, bushing, pin, wear pad or knob.
solution: Two things. First, a mobile print-and-machine unit (carbon-fiber nylon printing, benchtop CNC mill and lathe, handheld scanner) that turns a broken part into a fabricated one in hours. Second, a growing digital parts library indexed by machine make, model and serial number, where every repaired part becomes a reusable file. Farmers can also buy a 'Season Pass' per machine that guarantees fabricated-part turnaround inside 24 hours.
why_now: The FTC and five states settled with Deere on July 8, 2026. For 10 years Deere must give farmers and independent shops the same repair software and resources it gives dealers, and it separately agreed to a $99M class settlement. That will grow independent repair shops, and parts are the next bottleneck. Crop margins are tight, so cheaper aftermarket parts sell, and harvest is happening right now.
revenue_model: Per-part fabrication ($40 to $600, with a rush premium), Season Pass subscriptions ($1k to $2.5k per machine per season), wholesale to independent repair shops, and a co-op hosting fee or revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Farmers don't buy parts. They buy hours inside a weather window, so price against downtime avoided, not material cost. The scanned-part library by machine serial number is the compounding moat. Every emergency job builds the catalog that later lets you ship parts remotely, and the van is really a data-acquisition vehicle.
first_30_days: Borrow or rent a machine shop and start with two industrial printers, a benchtop mill and a scanner (about $40k to $60k), or begin with a used trailer. Sign two independent ag-repair shops and one co-op as hosts. Run a 'we fix it while you wait' pilot through the rest of this harvest, charging from job one. Post before/after photos in local farm Facebook groups and to elevator and co-op newsletters. Log every part as a file.

title: The Neutral Verdict on Dad's Driving
one_liner: An independent on-road evaluation of an aging parent's driving that gives adult children a credentialed Green, Yellow or Red verdict, plus a graduated plan so nobody has to be the villain about the keys.
customer: Adult children aged 45-65 of drivers 75+ pay $349-449 per evaluation and $12 a month for monitoring. Later buyers are auto insurers, Medicare Advantage plans and long-term-care insurers.
problem: Taking away the keys is one of the most dreaded family confrontations. The parent hears loss of independence and the child becomes the villain. Doctors rarely intervene, DMV medical review is slow, and driver-rehab specialists have months-long waitlists. Families wait for a crash. AAA and AARP offer generic tips, not an individual, defensible verdict.
solution: Frame it as a safety tune-up and send a certified evaluator, an OT with driver-rehab credentials or trained retired instructors under OT supervision. They ride in the parent's own car on a standardized 45-minute route with scoring for gap judgment, lane keeping, hesitation and scanning, plus a brief cognitive screen. The report gives a Green, Yellow or Red verdict. Yellow means no night, highway or rush hour with a recheck in six months, optionally verified by connected-car data or a cheap OBD dongle with the parent's consent. Red comes with a transition kit of robotaxi and rideshare credits, grocery and pharmacy delivery, and a senior-center pass, so retirement feels like an upgrade. The evaluator is advisory only and DMV referral is optional.
why_now: The oldest baby boomers turn 80 in 2026. Robotaxis now operate commercially in a growing list of US metros, so a real off-ramp finally exists. Connected-car APIs make objective driving data possible with consent. Scarce driver-rehab specialists can be leveraged with standardized scoring and remote review.
revenue_model: $349-449 per evaluation, a $12 monthly monitoring subscription for Yellow-zone drivers, and referral or ride-credit margin on the transition kit. B2B per-evaluation contracts with insurers and Medicare Advantage plans that want fewer elder-driver claims.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a third party who absorbs the blame. Families are buying relational insurance, not a road test. The recurring money is in the Yellow zone, where a graduated restriction plan needs ongoing verification, which turns a one-off confrontation into a subscription.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 driver-rehab OTs in one metro, plus elder-law attorneys and geriatric care managers for referrals. Build the scoring sheet from published road-test protocols. Get liability coverage and a consent script. Run 10 evaluations at a $249 intro price. Recruit through caregiver-support groups and Facebook groups for adult children of aging parents. Publish anonymized case studies.

title: Wildfire Evacuation Autopilot for Campsites and Hotels
one_liner: Satellite fire-spread alerts plus pre-contracted buses, routes and multilingual guest messaging turn every tourist lodging in fire country into an evacuation node.
customer: Campsites, holiday parks and hotels in fire-prone Mediterranean regions (France's Aude, Var and Gironde, Catalonia, Greece, Portugal, Croatia), plus regional tourism boards and insurers.
problem: Summer wildfires now force sudden evacuations of thousands of tourists who have no local knowledge, often no cars and no shared language. Duty of care sits with small operators holding paper plans they have never drilled, while insurers tighten terms.
solution: A site-specific evacuation plan with two routes and a refuge, ingestion of hourly fire detections (NASA FIRMS, Copernicus EFFIS and commercial satellite feeds), wind-aware fire arrival estimates per site, and automatic guest alerts by WhatsApp or SMS in the guest's language using check-in data. It includes a staff checklist and drills, and standby contracts with local coach operators.
why_now: Higher-frequency satellite fire detection arrived with early-2025 launches such as FireSat, and wildfire seasons in 2025 were severe across Southern Europe. Insurers and regulators are pressing small operators.
revenue_model: EUR 300-1,200 per site per year, margin on coach standby retainers, insurer premium-discount share and regional government contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Tourist lodging is the largest concentration of people in fire zones with no local knowledge, no vehicles and no common language, and the legal duty sits with operators who cannot afford risk consultants.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 campsites in Aude, Hérault, Var and Gironde through the camping federation. Deliver a plan PDF and WhatsApp alerts at EUR 390 per year, run one drill and pitch two insurers with results.

title: Under-Canopy Grave Detection Survey Service
one_liner: Find unmarked graves before the bulldozer does, using drone LiDAR that sees through trees, machine-learning triage and targeted ground-penetrating radar.
customer: Municipalities, state DOTs, developers, title companies, utilities and solar or pipeline builders, plus churches and heritage nonprofits.
problem: Lost and unrecorded burial grounds are usually discovered when earthmovers hit them, causing delay, cost and heartbreak. Historic cemeteries, especially those of marginalized communities, are often undocumented. GPR surveys are slow, costly per acre and limited by scarce operators. There is no burial-risk layer in due diligence.
solution: Drone LiDAR and photogrammetry across large tracts to detect depressions and anomalies under canopy, ML-ranked into a probability map, followed by targeted GPR verification of the top candidates. Deliver a survey report and a registry entry. Add LLM reading of handwritten cemetery and church records.
why_now: Survey-grade drone LiDAR is now cheap, ML for GPR and terrain anomalies has matured, and rural land is being cleared quickly for solar, data centers and pipelines. LLMs can now read handwritten historic records. Everstory's drone mapping of about 400 cemeteries shows the method works for known sites.
revenue_model: $200-$1,500 per acre depending on terrain and depth, annual subscriptions for DOTs and utilities, and data licensing to title insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Every earthmoving project carries burial-risk liability that appears in no database. The same survey serves developers, heritage groups and families, so it can be financed by the party with the most to lose.
first_30_days: Pilot with 2 churches or heritage groups on grant-funded work. Rent a LiDAR drone and pitch 5 solar developers on due-diligence add-ons. Recruit a GPR contractor and a cultural-resources archaeologist for sign-off.

title: Landowner-Side Broker for Data-Center Land
one_liner: A conflict-free advocate that scores your parcel's power value and runs a competitive process, so the family farm isn't sold cheap to an anonymous LLC.
customer: Family landowners with 100-2,000 acres near high-voltage transmission lines or substations, in data-center-active counties, who are getting unsolicited offers. Each deal is worth $5-50M or more.
problem: Developers approach landowners through shell LLCs and landmen, with NDAs and options that lock the land up cheaply. Landowners can't tell whether $30K or $300K an acre is fair, because value now depends on grid interconnection position, water and fiber rather than acreage. Regional brokers don't know how to value power, so owners either sell too low or refuse offers that are actually good.
solution: A licensed landowner-side brokerage. A Parcel Power Score built from public transmission and substation data, utility large-load tariffs, zoning and moratorium status, water and fiber proximity, and an independent power engineer's review. It runs a competitive process to many site-selection teams and developers, negotiates terms (sale, option, lease, JV, decommissioning bonds), and represents only the seller.
why_now: Land purchases for future data centers reached about $6B in the first half of 2026, up roughly 79% from a year earlier (Avison Young), and sale offers in some places run up to 10 times agricultural value. Sept 2026 coverage shows farmers getting huge offers alongside a local backlash and moratoria that make timing and zoning risk decisive. The seller-side infrastructure has not caught up.
revenue_model: $5-15K representation retainer that is credited against a 1-2% success fee. On $10-50M deals this is $100-500K per closing. Optional fee for a second-opinion review of an existing offer.
non_obvious_insight: Land in this market is priced on power queue position, not soil. Buyers know it and sellers don't, and that information gap is the fee pool. Being seller-only and publishing the methodology makes you the trusted party for landowners and gives hyperscalers a pre-assembled, pre-screened pipeline they will actually prefer. The parcel data is a compounding asset.
first_30_days: Pick a cluster of counties around a substation or 345kV corridor in a data-center-active area (for example Ohio, Indiana, Georgia, Texas or Pennsylvania). Build parcel maps with public HIFLD and county data. Mail or door-knock 300 landowners with a free Parcel Power Score. Partner with a rural land attorney and an independent power engineer, get a broker license or partner with a licensed broker, and aim to sign 3 exclusive representation agreements. Send a one-page buyer package to 20 site-selection teams.

title: Sell the Route, Not the Business
one_liner: A standardized customer-book sale with a retention earn-out held in escrow and released automatically from payment data.
customer: Owner-operators aged 58+ of recurring-revenue routes with $80-500k revenue (pool, lawn, pest, cleaning, snow, window, HVAC maintenance, small bookkeeping and tax practices), and 5-30 employee competitors nearby who would buy them.
problem: No broker will list a $150k-revenue business, so retiring owners walk away and customers scatter. Buyers can't verify retention and the parties fight over price. Search funds target $5-50M companies and nothing serves the sub-$1M tier.
solution: Package the asset as the recurring customer relationship, not the entity. The product supplies consented customer-list transfer, a standard purchase agreement, a pricing multiple on trailing recurring revenue, and a 12-month retention earn-out held in escrow that releases as Stripe, QuickBooks or bank data confirms customers still pay. It adds customer-notice and handover-ride workflows, a non-compete, and matching to nearby operators. SBA Express lender partners finance the buyer.
why_now: From July 2026 an SBA 7(a) can be combined with a 504 for up to $10M, which loosens acquisition credit. Payment data now makes retention measurable in real time. An aging owner cohort meets flat CPA supply on the bookkeeping side.
revenue_model: 5-8% success fee to seller and buyer, plus escrow and retention-tracking fees, plus referral fees from lenders and insurers.
non_obvious_insight: At this size nobody needs to find a buyer for the business, because the natural buyer is the competitor with trucks two zip codes away. Retention escrow turns the valuation argument into a measured outcome.
first_30_days: Choose one vertical (for example pool routes) in one metro. Broker three deals by hand through Facebook groups and route-broker forums using a lawyer-drafted standard contract and Stripe Connect escrow. Document time to close and retention, then productize the paperwork.

title: Tech-to-Owner Buyout Kit for Trade Shops
one_liner: Package and finance the sale of sub-$5M trade shops to their own senior technicians or managers, then keep them on a shared back office so the acquired shop does not stall.
customer: Retiring owners of 5-40 person HVAC, plumbing, electrical and roofing shops that PE roll-ups skip, plus their number-two techs or GMs and SBA lenders.
problem: McKinsey says 6M small businesses face ownership transitions by 2035 and a third of owners over 50 struggle to find a buyer. PE pays 10-14x EBITDA for platforms above $25M revenue but only 2-3.5x for small owner-operators, a 3-5x valuation gap. When the small shop closes, its crew and customers vanish, deepening the trades shortage.
solution: A deal factory: clean financials from QuickBooks and field-service exports, SBA 7(a) plus seller-note packaging, a 90-day transition playbook, license-qualifier continuity, and a fractional-CFO and shared back office (payroll, purchasing group, bidding) for the new owner. A short cohort teaches buyer-techs finance, hiring and pricing.
why_now: PE buying spree (Apollo/Apex, Blackstone/Champions, Bain/Service Logic) raises the visible price of scale but skips small shops. The silver-tsunami timeline is now. Roofing is the least consolidated trade and ServiceTitan is deprioritizing it, so owners have fewer software-led growth options.
revenue_model: 3-5% success fee on the deal. $2-4K per month shared back-office subscription for 24-36 months.
non_obvious_insight: The best buyer for a small shop is not PE or a stranger, it is the employee who already knows the customers, trucks and quirks. What is missing is packaging, seller financing and post-close operating support. Every closed shop deletes 5-20 tradespeople from a scarce local supply, which makes preservation valuable to the community.
first_30_days: Pick one trade in one metro. Cold-outreach 200 owners aged 58+ from state license databases with a free 30-minute valuation chat. Sign three exclusive listings, identify the tech buyers via the owners, and line up two SBA lenders.

title: Worker-Ownership Succession for Home Care Agencies
one_liner: A specialist shop that helps retiring home-care agency owners sell to their caregivers via an ESOP or worker co-op, plus a shared back office for the converted agencies.
customer: Owners aged 58-72 of $2-15M revenue home-care agencies with no successor. CDFI lenders and employee-ownership funds are financing partners.
problem: Reimbursement is squeezed (a 1.3% aggregate cut for CY2026, with a -3.0% temporary adjustment still in place), private-equity money goes to software and big platforms, and even UnitedHealth had to divest 164 Amedisys locations. Small owners have no buyer, while agencies lose 77-80% of caregivers a year.
solution: A conversion shop: valuation, readiness (licensure and payer change-of-ownership rules), structure (S-corp ESOP, worker co-op or employee-ownership trust), financing (seller note plus CDFI or SBA), and a two-year ownership-culture program (caregiver equity, profit sharing, scheduling voice). Converted agencies share a back office (payroll, billing, EVV, recruiting).
why_now: Boomer owners are retiring into a weak sales market after the 2026 rate squeeze, and the workforce shortage means the workforce is the scarcest asset. Cooperative Home Care Associates in the Bronx shows the model works.
revenue_model: Transaction fee of 3-5% of deal value, $8-15k a month back-office fees, and a small share of network EBITDA.
non_obvious_insight: In a business where turnover is the profit killer, the best buyer for a struggling agency is the workforce itself. Ownership is a retention tool, and the exit-plan angle sells to owners who don't care about culture.
first_30_days: Work with a state home-care association to get 20 owner conversations. Sell five $12k ownership-readiness assessments, line up a CDFI lender, and target first LOI within six months.

title: Cryo-Vault for Artisan Food Microbial Cultures
one_liner: Backup-and-rescue service that fingerprints, isolates and cryo-banks the living house cultures (cheese rind flora, koji, kombucha SCOBYs, sourdough starters, mushroom spawn, natural-wine yeast) of small food producers in split-geography -80 storage, with a 48-hour emergency revival.
customer: Small artisan producers: raw-milk and farmstead cheesemakers, koji, miso and sake makers, kombucha brewers, specialty mushroom growers, sourdough bakeries, natural winemakers and cideries. Pay $250-400 intake plus $20-40/month per culture, and $400-600 per emergency rescue.
problem: A small producer's house culture is their product identity, yet it lives on the counter or in a single fridge, propagated by serial subculture. Mother cultures senesce and drift, contaminate, or get wiped out by phage (dairy) or Trichoderma-type molds (mushrooms). One crash can end a brand for months. Big culture houses won't bank a small producer's strains, and commercial biobank services are priced and designed for pharma.
solution: A mail-in kit: send a gram of culture, get back an ITS/16S-based composition fingerprint, viability and purity report, and isolated key strains. Each is banked as glycerol stocks in triplicate at two separate sites, with a dashboard of banked cultures. The rescue tier revives a viable working culture in 48 hours with contamination diagnosis, and later adds a periodic 'drift check' compared against the banked baseline. Optional fingerprint certificates for craft-authenticity claims and geographic-indication programs.
why_now: Fermentation and koji-based craft food is booming, and sequencing costs are trivial (about $30 per amplicon sample). Consolidation and climate stress are raising the cost of a culture crash. Small food makers increasingly market on 'living' and heritage claims that they can't currently back up. Laid-off microbiologists can staff this cheaply.
revenue_model: Intake fee plus recurring monthly vault subscription per culture. Per-event rescue fees. Fingerprint certificates and drift-check add-ons. Later B2B with food-safety consultants and craft trade associations, which bundle it as a member benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Cryo-banking with a genetic fingerprint is routine bench hygiene for any wet-lab, but the food world has never been offered it at a price small producers can pay. Nobody thinks of 'my sourdough' as a strain to back up until it crashes. The wedge is not the science, it is the packaging as insurance and the rescue promise.
first_30_days: Bank 10 cultures for free from friendly producers (cheesemakers, kombucha and mushroom growers) recruited through guild forums and Facebook groups. Rent -80 space at a university core, a co-lab or a local biobank. Use a commercial amplicon sequencing service for fingerprints. Publish one story about a rescued culture. Convert the first cohort to $99/month founding-member pricing. Stay strictly with BSL-1 food-grade organisms and set clear policies on pathogen refusal and shipping.

title: Canary Humans: Leak-Testing ID Verification Vendors
one_liner: Put consenting, instrumented real people through a platform's ID and age checks, then prove whether the vendor kept, leaked or resold their documents.
customer: Trust-and-safety, privacy and vendor-risk leads at platforms that outsource ID or age checks (dating apps, gig and rental marketplaces, cannabis and vape retail tech, crypto exchanges, adult and gaming operators), and the cyber insurers underwriting them.
problem: Platforms pick verification vendors on a SOC 2 badge and a promise to delete images quickly, and customers cannot test that promise. AU10TIX, Discord's support vendor, Persona and IDScan were all breached in 2024-26. IDScan reported 150M+ licence scans stolen in Sept 2026. Ofcom and state AGs judge platforms on 'reasonable steps', so the platform owns its vendor's failure.
solution: Recruit a few hundred paid 'canary humans' with unique emails, phones, addresses and ID numbers, and enrol them in the customer's live verification flow with the customer's consent. Then run scheduled tests: deletion requests, access requests to the vendor and its sub-processors, and monitoring of breach dumps, data-broker files, phishing and spam lists and dark-market listings for canary-unique strings. The deliverable is a quarterly retention and leakage attestation with evidence, usable in vendor contracts, cyber-insurance applications and regulator files. It also produces a public 'retention half-life' benchmark by vendor.
why_now: IDScan's Sept 2026 breach (150M+ licences) and the Persona, AU10TIX and Discord-vendor incidents showed that certified vendors leak. The EU's 31 Dec 2026 age-verification rollout deadline will push thousands more sites to outsource checks. Ofcom has opened 90+ investigations and issued fines. The Delve scandal (Mar-Apr 2026) showed that paper compliance is not proof.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per platform per vendor tested, an insurer portfolio programme (per-insured fee), and a breach-forensics retainer. Later add an efficacy-proof product for privacy-removal services.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance automation (Vanta is at roughly $300M ARR) certifies that controls exist on paper, and nobody tests outcomes. A verifier's product is a promise to forget, and the only way to audit a promise about data is to plant traceable data and watch where it surfaces. Security calls these honeytokens and direct marketers call them seed lists, but nobody has applied the trick to verification vendors.
first_30_days: Recruit 50 privacy-minded volunteers at $100-200 each with signed consent and a legal review (no fake IDs, real people only). Pitch three mid-size dating, gig or cannabis-tech platforms and one cyber MGA. Offer a free 90-day pilot against one vendor under NDA. Publish an anonymised benchmark from the pilot to generate inbound.

title: Robotaxi Escort: Curb-to-Exam-Room Concierge
one_liner: Trained escorts who meet seniors at the door, ride the robotaxi with them, wait at the appointment and bring them home, replacing costly NEMT vehicles.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans with transport benefits, adult children, life-plan communities and hospital discharge teams, at about $45-60 per escorted round trip.
problem: Robotaxis carry about 500k paid rides a week in 10+ metros, but a frail rider cannot handle the app, curb boarding or a walker, and cannot find the right entrance. Traditional non-emergency medical transport with vans and drivers costs $90-150 a trip and is unreliable.
solution: Unbundle NEMT. The autonomous car supplies the vehicle and the driver-free miles, and the escort supplies only the missing human parts: booking on the senior's behalf, door-through-door help, walker stowage, waiting and handoff to clinic staff. Family members receive live trip updates and fraud-safe spending limits.
why_now: Waymo is at about 3,900 vehicles with fares from Zoox starting Aug 2026. Seniors now hold Medicaid and MA transport benefits that plans want to cut costs on.
revenue_model: Per-trip fee ($45-60 escort plus ride cost passed through) or $199 a month family subscription. Gross margin of 35-45% after escort wages.
non_obvious_insight: Robotaxis remove the driver but not the need for a helper at each end. Whoever provides that helper owns the senior segment, and no fleet operator wants to.
first_30_days: Launch in one Waymo metro (Phoenix or Austin) with 10 escorts recruited from nursing students and retirees. Sign five independent-living communities and two geriatric clinics for private-pay trips. Then approach an MA plan's transport benefit team with trip logs.

title: Reefer Claim Vault for Small Carriers
one_liner: An always-on evidence recorder that captures the proof that decides cargo claims, giving small carriers and their cargo insurers a one-click defense packet.
customer: Small reefer and dry-van carriers (1 to 50 trucks), especially produce and protein lanes, and the cargo-insurance agencies and MGAs that write them. Brokers needing reefer-specific carrier diligence are a secondary buyer.
problem: Small carriers lose or pay $5k to $60k cargo claims not because they were at fault but because they can't prove it. Pre-cool temperature, setpoint, continuous versus cycle-sentry mode, who loaded and counted, and seal integrity all decide a Carmack claim, and the evidence is usually never captured or gets overwritten on the reefer unit. After a claim, the cargo insurer raises rates or cancels. Post-Montgomery, reefer-specific vetting is also becoming a standard-of-care question for brokers.
solution: A driver app with a 90-second guided pickup ritual: photo of the empty trailer floor and reefer display, pre-cool temp, setpoint and mode, seal photo before the forklift touches it, an OCR check of the BOL that flags a missing 'SL&C' (shipper load and count) notation, seal number or temp instructions, and a Bluetooth probe reading of product temperature at load. It pulls continuous temperature records from reefer telematics (Thermo King, Carrier) or a $30 BLE data logger and hash-timestamps everything. When a claim lands, it generates a Carmack-structured defense packet in one click. Insurers get aggregate loss-prevention scoring by carrier.
why_now: The 2026 Montgomery ruling has brokers and insurers paying attention to reefer diligence. Cargo losses and theft are up sharply (Verisk CargoNet Q2 2026 losses of $304.6M). Vision AI makes BOL and photo checking cheap, and reefer telematics APIs and cheap Bluetooth loggers have matured.
revenue_model: $25 to $40 per truck per month for carriers. MGAs and agencies pay $10 per truck per month or fund the subscription in exchange for loss-ratio improvement and premium credits. A $150 flat fee per claim-defense packet for non-subscribers as a low-friction entry.
non_obvious_insight: Claims are decided by paper nobody produced in the sixty seconds when it mattered. Every veteran knows the ritual: write SL&C on the BOL, photograph the seal before anyone touches the door, snap the pre-cool, and download the reefer unit before it rolls over. Nobody does it consistently because nobody reminds them at the dock. Insurers see the losses but not the cause, so they will pay to change driver behavior at the moment of pickup.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 small cargo-insurance agencies that specialize in trucking. Recruit 20 reefer carriers hauling produce (Fresno to Nogales, Yakima, Salinas). Give them a free 30-day pilot plus the BLE logger at cost. Build a PWA using photo capture and Claude vision for BOL checks. Track claim outcomes on pilot trucks versus a control group to build the insurer's business case.

title: Patent-Grade Variant Maps for Biologics
one_liner: Pooled-screening service that generates the sequence-function data biologics patents now need after Amgen v. Sanofi, plus a mirror-image design-around report for companies facing sequence claims.
customer: IP counsel and patent boutiques at antibody and protein biotechs, biosimilar and biobetter developers, and mid-size biotechs working in crowded target classes.
problem: Trend chain: Amgen v. Sanofi (2023) killed functional genus antibody claims unless the specification enables the full scope. Patents therefore shrink toward sequence-specific claims backed by data. Counsel typically has data on 20-50 variants. Meanwhile cheap DNA and AI design make thousands of function-preserving variants easy to produce, so both breadth-by-data (offense) and design-around (defense) become experimental problems that no one packages.
solution: Offense: pooled display or mammalian screening of 10^4-10^6 designed variants with NGS readout, delivered as patent-ready sequence-function tables and generalizations (which CDR positions tolerate what) to support broader claims. Defense: search patent sequence claims, compute identity against claim thresholds, design function-preserving escapes and validate the top candidates in a pool. Sold through IP counsel, not legal advice.
why_now: DNA is no longer the cost: Weizmann built 2.5 billion antibody fragments on phage for EUR 38,000 of DNA. Zero-shot design tools generate variants at scale. Post-Amgen enablement pressure has had three years to bite, and law-firm commentary is now explicitly tackling AI and enablement.
revenue_model: $40-150k per patent family for offense work, $8-25k per FTO or design-around candidate, and subscriptions for boutiques.
non_obvious_insight: With cheap DNA and pooled assays, 'enablement by data' becomes a commodity for whoever runs the experiment. Patent breadth turns into a function of wet-lab throughput rather than lawyer cleverness. The same machine that broadens your claims also narrows a competitor's, so buyers exist on both sides of every thicket.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IP boutiques as design partners. Build a claim-matching tool on public USPTO and EPO sequence listings. Offer 10 free FTO scans. Contract a pooled-display partner. Price one paid offense pilot with a biotech preparing a continuation filing.

title: Independent audit desk for city surveillance vendors
one_liner: A fixed-price monthly service that checks whether a city's license-plate-reader and drone vendor is actually following the city's own sharing rules, and hands the council a report it can cite.
customer: City auditors, city attorneys and city managers (plus police oversight boards) in the roughly 50+ cities that cancelled or suspended Flock and the many more that kept ALPR or drone programs under new council conditions. Buyers pay $1.2k-2.5k/month per city from the auditor, city attorney or IT budget, well under the informal-procurement threshold.
problem: Cities cannot verify what the surveillance vendor does with their data. Mountain View's own audit found a statewide-lookup setting active on 29 of 30 cameras since program start, with 250+ outside agencies running about 600,000 searches in 12 months, and the vendor kept no records that would show what was shared. Oxnard's vendor silently re-enabled a nationwide query feature. Evanston found cameras reinstalled after cancellation. Dayton found 7,100+ searches for immigration enforcement that city policy prohibited. Councils now write audit duties into ordinances, but the auditor's office has no tooling.
solution: A vendor-neutral audit service (Flock, Axon, Motorola/Vigilant, drone platforms). The city exports the search and audit logs and sharing-settings screenshots it can already download. The service ingests them and runs a rules engine against the city's adopted policy: searches with no case number or with vague reason codes, out-of-state or federal agencies, immigration-related terms, off-hours spikes, and diffs of the network-sharing settings month to month to catch silent config changes. Output is a council-ready quarterly report and a same-week alert on config drift. Add-on: a field check that cameras a council ordered off are really off, since Evanston found them reinstalled.
why_now: 53 cities across 20 states had cancelled or rejected Flock by mid-2026 over unauthorized federal access. New state laws (Colorado SB 26-070 warrant rule, Washington SB 6002, Kentucky HB 58 90-day retention cap, Maine's ALPR law) add compliance duties. Atlanta's ordinance, held in committee and taken up again in September 2026, would require monthly internal access audits and annual independent technical audits managed by the City Auditor. Drone-as-first-responder approvals (Stockton, Federal Way, Santa Fe, Whittier) are expanding the audit surface.
revenue_model: $4.5k one-time baseline configuration and log audit, then $1.2k-2.5k/month monitoring and quarterly council report. Upsell: annual independent technical audit that ordinances like Atlanta's require, priced $15k-40k for larger cities. Multi-year contracts through city auditor offices.
non_obvious_insight: The market is created by oversight ordinances, not by the surveillance vendors. Every ordinance that says 'audit monthly' is an unfunded mandate on a three-person auditor's office, and the failure mode is configuration drift, not sophisticated data science. Evidence: Mountain View's statewide lookup ran from launch until Jan 5, 2026 unnoticed (https://www.mv-voice.com/police/2026/01/30/amid-immigration-crackdown-mountain-view-discovers-unauthorized-access-to-license-plate-data/). The audit findings and 53-city cancellation count are in https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319317/20260629/flock-safety-crosses-100000-cameras-53-cities-cancel-over-unauthorized-federal-data-access.htm. Atlanta's proposed monthly internal and annual independent audits are at https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/09/22/atlanta-weighs-sweeping-rules-monthly-audits-surveillance-tech/. New Hanover County's commissioners called for 'explicit guardrails' before restoring cameras: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9840468/north-carolina/new-hanover-county/commissioners-cite-privacy-shifting-vendor-policies-and-misuse-when-cancelling-flock-alpr-contract. Cities that keep the cameras need proof of compliance to survive the next council vote, and the audit report is that proof.
first_30_days: File public-records requests in about 25 cities that cancelled or kept ALPR for the audit-log export format and sharing-settings history, and build a parser for it. Produce one free 'configuration drift' teardown for a friendly city attorney or a councilmember who championed the cancellation. Pitch the $4.5k baseline audit to auditors and attorneys in cities with surveillance-oversight ordinances (Seattle, San Diego, Oakland, Cambridge, Urbana) and to those now drafting them (Atlanta). Sign 3 pilots. Main risk: vendor cooperation and export formats, so start with cities that already run their own audits.

title: Court-Ready Smoke Testing Protocol for Fire Survivors
one_liner: A standardized smoke and ash sampling protocol plus lab network that satisfies California's new smoke-damage presumption law, sold to public adjusters, policyholders and eventually carriers.
customer: Public adjusters, policyholder attorneys and restoration contractors handling open LA and Southern California fire claims, paying $1,200-3,500 per home. Carriers and TPAs are a later channel, since the law makes testing an insurer-funded cost.
problem: Fire survivors have fought carriers for months or years over whether smoke-contaminated homes are safe. There is no agreed testing or restoration standard, so each claim becomes a fight between competing consultants. The new law shifts testing cost to insurers and blocks Additional Living Expense from ending until homes are restored and safe.
solution: A published sampling protocol and chain-of-custody workflow run by certified industrial hygienists and partner labs. It produces a report format mapped to the statute's language (presumption, testing funded by insurers, pre-loss restoration). We bundle software that generates the sampling plan, tracks lab results, and drafts the repair scope. Sell to public adjusters first, then offer carriers a neutral-standard option.
why_now: AB 1795 was signed on 2026-09-15 and introduces a smoke-damage presumption, insurer-paid testing and sampling, inspection and claims-handling timelines, and adjuster training. The industry group APCIA asked that guidance be 'grounded in credible science, valid methodologies.' SB 876, signed 2026-09-28 and effective 2027-01-01, doubles penalties for unfair claims practices during declared emergencies and requires insurers to file disaster recovery plans, raising the stakes on slow claims.
revenue_model: Per-home testing and reporting fee of $1,200-3,500. Software seats for public adjusters at $200-400 per month. Later a per-claim neutral-testing fee from carriers and TPAs, and lab partnership revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The law creates a paid testing mandate without naming a standard, so whoever defines the accepted protocol captures the spend. Evidence: https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/west/2026/09/15/885209.htm (presumption, insurer-paid testing, ALE protections; APCIA's 'credible science' quote; contentious smoke claims after the 2025 LA fires) and https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/release031-2026.cfm (Commissioner Lara: families 'have spent months, and sometimes years, fighting over whether their homes were safe'). https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release034-2026.cfm covers SB 876, including doubled penalties in emergencies and a 15-day adjuster-change update. Public adjusters have no neutral, repeatable science kit today, and carriers lose in disputes when their own hired consultant is the only standard.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 certified industrial hygienists and 1 accredited lab in the LA area. Draft the protocol from published standards and the statute text. Offer 10 public adjusters with open Eaton and Palisades claims a discounted first three homes in exchange for case studies. Invite APCIA member claim managers to review the protocol for credibility.

title: Shared Emergency Desk for Autonomous Fleets
one_liner: A neutral 24/7 first-responder interface (hotline, dispatch API, geofence directives) that small AV, robot-truck and delivery-robot operators rent instead of building.
customer: Newer and second-tier AV operators (autonomous trucking, shuttles, delivery pods, robotaxi entrants), and city and county 911 dispatch centers on the public-facing side.
problem: Regulators are asking for a human phone number, not more autonomy. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on July 8, 2026, and California's AV enforcement rules take effect in 2026 (as I understand them). Waymo alone runs about 70 remote agents per shift from two centers in the Philippines, which small operators cannot copy.
solution: A US-staffed desk trained on fire and police protocols. It offers standardized emergency-response guides, one API through which dispatch centers can stop, unlock or reroute any subscribing fleet, compliance logs, and drills for first responders.
why_now: Driverless trucking is commercial (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k driverless orders, Einride listed), new AV entrants are launching, and states are writing rules. Compliance deadlines land in 2026.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per vehicle per year or an $8-25k monthly fleet retainer, plus training contracts with cities.
non_obvious_insight: A commodity BPO with liability attached scales with vehicle count, and neutrality is a feature because cities prefer one interface for all fleets. Large operators build their own desks, so the long tail of new entrants is the market.
first_30_days: Interview 10 safety and compliance leads at autonomous trucking and delivery-robot companies. Build a minimal hotline plus web console for a single pilot, co-design the protocol with 2 city or county dispatch centers, and sign 2 paid pilots at about $5k a month.

title: Install-and-Map Crew for Crowdfunded Yard Robots
one_liner: A local white-glove setup and seasonal-care service for the $4-5K yard robots that Kickstarter backers are buying and struggling to get working.
customer: Owners of $2,200-$5,500 crowdfunded or prosumer yard robots (Yarbo M and similar): affluent suburban homeowners with 0.5-2 acres, seniors who cannot lift a 200 lb unit, and small landscaping and snow-removal firms. Payer is the homeowner or firm, with an installer-referral fee from manufacturers or resellers as a later option.
problem: Big-ticket crowdfunded robots ship as a Shenzhen-supported product that takes multiple weekends to set up: RTK antenna placement, GPS calibration, yard mapping, no-go zones, firmware chasing. It weighs about 200 lb, and owners report escalations without resolution from a China-based support team.
solution: A certified two-person install crew that does a one-visit RTK site survey (satellite-visibility check, antenna mounting), lifts and assembles the unit, maps the yard, sets zones and snow paths, and hands off with a 30-day check-in. Add a $19/mo seasonal-care plan covering firmware updates, blade and attachment swaps, and pre-winter snow-blower setup. Start with Yarbo, then extend to other $3K+ crowdfunded home robots and ultra-short-throw laser projectors (5,260 backers took the $2,999 XGIMI tier).
why_now: Yarbo M backers were told to expect delivery from August 2026, and snow-blower-module backers ship mid-November, right before the season the module exists for. That gives a hard deadline in autumn 2026. Wire-free RTK robots are only now cheap enough for homeowners, and the seniors and heavy-yard buyers who most need help are exactly the ones who cannot self-install.
revenue_model: $399-$799 per install visit (higher for wooded or complex lots), $19/mo or $149/yr seasonal-care plan, and $99-$199 per attachment swap or spring/fall visit. Optional B2B contracts for landscapers converting to robot fleets.
non_obvious_insight: The Kickstarter tech median pledge is $194, but this robot's backers average over $4,000 each ($3,158,140 from 751 backers, https://www.gizmocrowd.com/post/yarbo-m-yard-robot). At that price the buyer is effectively a serviced-equipment customer, not a gadget hobbyist. Hands-on reviews say setup took multiple weekends, the unit weighs about 200 lb (owners "could not have set the unit up alone"), GPS struggles under tree cover, support runs from China with East Coast friction, and the maker declined Home Assistant API access in March 2025 (https://seekandscore.com/yarbo-review/). Crowdfunded hardware makers optimise for shipping units, not last-mile success, so the installer layer is unowned. It is a local-services business with software-like repeat revenue.
first_30_days: Read public Kickstarter and Yarbo forum comments to find backers in snow-belt ZIP codes, and post in the Yarbo owner communities offering a founding-customer $299 install. Recruit 2-3 landscapers or handymen who already own a truck and lift gear. Run 5 paid installs on your own or friends' properties to write a mapping and RTK-survey checklist, then film one before/after case study. Book 15-20 installs timed to the November snow-blower shipments and sign one landscaping firm to a pilot contract.

title: Payment-Slip Doctor for Foreign Residents
one_liner: A LINE service that lets a foreign resident photograph a Japanese payment slip or government letter and get a plain explanation, deadline, consequences and payment help in their own language.
customer: Japanese-language schools, vocational schools and universities with many foreign students, at about ¥300 per student per month. Later customers are municipal national-health-insurance departments paying for improved collection, employers of foreign staff, and rent-guarantee and property-management firms.
problem: Foreign residents paid on average only 63% of national health insurance premiums by the end of 2024, according to a survey of about 150 local governments. From around FY2027, unpaid premiums and pension contributions will be a ground to deny visa renewal or change of status. Yet at my counter, foreign customers regularly hand me a slip or official letter and ask what it means. The barcode on a konbini payment slip is void after the due date, so I have to refuse it. Then a worker who cannot get to the ward office in daytime faces an arrears spiral that may end in a denied visa. The government mails a notice in Japanese that looks like junk mail.
solution: Photograph the slip or letter. The service reads the barcode and text, identifies the document type such as national health insurance, resident tax, pension or traffic fine, and explains in Vietnamese, Nepali, Chinese, Burmese or Indonesian what it is, how much, when due, and the consequences of non-payment. It sets calendar reminders and links to pay by PayPay, bank app or konbini. If the slip is expired, it generates a reissue script and shows ward-office hours and the nearest late-opening branch. Anything ambiguous or legal is escalated to a partner administrative scrivener. Stickers with a QR code at konbini payment counters are the acquisition channel.
why_now: The 2026 system upgrades that will link municipal payment records to Immigration Services Agency data, plus the rule that unpaid premiums will block renewals from around 2027, make payment compliance a visa issue for hundreds of thousands of students and workers. The current government has made foreign-resident rule enforcement a political priority. Schools are already adding payment-tracking features to their student systems. Nobody has built the explanation layer, and translation apps do not decode payment slips or their deadlines.
revenue_model: Schools pay ¥300-500 per student per month. Municipalities pay per successful on-time payment or a share of recovered arrears. Employers pay per foreign employee per month. Property managers and guarantors pay per tenant. A small paid human-escalation tier costs the user ¥980 per case.
non_obvious_insight: The failure point is not language in general. It is a single document, the konbini payment slip, and a single hidden rule that its barcode dies on the due date. People miss it by a day and the consequence is a visa problem. The counter clerk sees this daily, so the demand is proven and concentrated. Because the buyer of the outcome is a school or municipality, the paying customer is not the end user.
first_30_days: Build the LINE OA with barcode decoding, OCR and slip-type rules for the five most common slips, and Vietnamese, Nepali and Chinese output reviewed by native speakers. Put QR stickers on the payment counters of my three stores. Pilot with two Osaka language schools, about 300 students, at ¥300 per student per month. Measure on-time payment before and after. Bring the results to one ward's national health insurance department. Partner with an administrative scrivener firm for the escalation tier.

title: Verified Gig Work History via Data-Access Rights
one_liner: Use statutory data-access requests as an API to pull couriers' and drivers' records from platforms, and issue a verified work-history credential they can carry to landlords, lenders and rival platforms.
customer: Couriers, ride-hail drivers, hosts and cleaners in the EU and UK are the users. Payers are letting agents and landlords, credit unions, neobanks and car-leasing firms verifying variable income, and platforms new to a city that want to import proven riders.
problem: Gig income and ratings are locked in platform apps. Screenshots are unverifiable, so lenders and landlords reject workers or demand guarantors. Changing platforms resets reputation to zero, and deactivations are opaque.
solution: An Export Desk. The worker signs a mandate. The service files GDPR access and portability requests to each platform (and requests under the Platform Work Directive as national laws land), normalizes the data into a standard schema, cross-checks it against bank statements, and issues a signed Work History Credential. It carries tenure, 12-month net income with variance, rating percentile, hours and deactivation events, and it can be shared by link or QR with selective disclosure. Pooled volume gives workers a bargaining bloc.
why_now: The EU Platform Work Directive must be transposed by 2 December 2026, and the Commission says no delay is possible. It strengthens workers' rights to information about algorithmic management. Italy has a draft law, Germany and Spain are moving, and the data-access rights already exist under GDPR and UK GDPR.
revenue_model: Free for workers. Lenders and letting agents pay $6-15 per verified pack, new-entrant platforms pay $20-40 per imported worker, and workers can pay about $4 a month for auto-refresh.
non_obvious_insight: When platforms will not offer an API, the statute is the API. Response clocks are slow but predictable. Once thousands of workers use it, platforms will want to build real APIs to avoid processing requests, and you become the neutral verifier they must integrate with.
first_30_days: Partner with a couriers' or drivers' union or a worker-data nonprofit. Onboard 100 couriers in London or Amsterdam. Produce 50 verified packs by filing requests and reconciling with bank data. Sign two letting agents or a credit union to accept the packs as an alternative to guarantors for a pilot.

title: Shelved-Game Rescue Exchange
one_liner: A broker that packages cancelled and orphaned game prototypes and licenses them to laid-off veteran teams on revenue-share terms, with reversion rights if the game stalls.
customer: Publishers, closing studios and insolvency administrators holding unreleased builds (they get a recovery instead of a write-off). The paying counterparties are veteran-led small teams and the funders behind them.
problem: Ubisoft cancelled six games in Jan 2026 and cut headcount from 18,666 to 16,590. EA's owners closed a $55B LBO with $20B of debt and a stated plan to cut costs with AI. Cancelled projects sit unused with teams disbanded, while laid-off veterans have skills but no IP or prototype budget.
solution: Build a 'prototype data room' per project: build, design docs, and a third-party licence and music clearance audit. Add a standard rescue licence (revenue share, milestone reversion, credit terms) and a registry of veteran team leads. Match the two, and offer milestone-funded finishing through a small fund or partner investors. Start with insolvent and small publishers, which move faster than Ubisoft or EA legal.
why_now: The 2023-26 layoff wave left an unusually deep bench of finished-quality talent. The EA LBO and Ubisoft restructuring guarantee more shelved work. Steam distribution and Epic's 0% fee on the first $1M make a 10-20 person finish economically viable.
revenue_model: 10-15% of the licensee's revenue share, or a success fee at signing ($10-50k), plus a data-room packaging fee paid by the rights holder.
non_obvious_insight: A shelved game's cost to its owner is legal and opportunity overhead, not the code. A zero-upfront licence with reversion beats a write-down and avoids a public fire sale. Insiders assume cancelled means bad, but many projects die for portfolio or budget-cycle reasons, not quality.
first_30_days: Publish a public 'orphaned prototypes wanted' page. Call 20 insolvency administrators and mid-size publishers found through recent studio-closure announcements with a one-page offer. Have a games lawyer draft the rescue licence. Recruit 10 veteran-led teams from layoff communities on Discord and LinkedIn. Aim for one signed rescue by day 60.

title: AI-Washing Forensics for Investors and Buyers
one_liner: A five-day outside-in diligence product that tests whether an AI startup's product is real autonomy, its revenue is real, and its users are human.
customer: Seed-to-growth investors (micro-VCs, corporate VCs, growth funds), corporate M&A teams, venture lenders, and enterprise procurement teams buying AI vendors.
problem: Builder.ai's 2025 insolvency (marketed AI, with heavy human labour behind it), the 2025 DOJ case against the founder of Nate, and a wave of 'ARR' made of pilots, credits and bot traffic show that diligence rests on demos, reference calls and a quality-of-earnings that never tests the technology claim.
solution: A black-box harness and data-room protocol. It covers interaction testing at scale (latency and variance signatures that reveal human-in-the-loop or third-party model calls), unit-economics reconstruction (tokens versus price versus gross margin), revenue reality (read-only Stripe and bank data plus contract sampling to separate pilot, committed, credit-funded and refunded revenue), audience authenticity (bot and agent share of users from server logs), and independent reference call-backs. Output is a 'Reality Report' with confidence intervals.
why_now: Builder.ai (2025) and Delve (2026) reset investor trust. AI-startup ARR claims are exploding, and more than half of web traffic is now automated, which inflates 'users'. Investors are compressing diligence to days, and AI products are uniquely testable from outside because you can hit the endpoint.
revenue_model: $15-40k per full report paid by the investor (often reimbursed at close), a $5k lite scan, and annual portfolio-monitoring retainers for funds.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume diligence must rely on the founder's data. AI products can be tested from the outside, so the scarce thing is independence and speed, and the buyer of speed is an investor with a 48-hour exclusivity window.
first_30_days: Offer five free 'reality scans' to angel syndicates and micro-VC partners on live deals in exchange for named case studies. Build the harness with two ML engineers and one forensic accountant. Set pricing after three wins.
